about: How `-x` tokens bind. A short flag taking a value accepts it attached, attached after `=`, or as the following word. Several value-less shorts may be bundled in one token.

vectors.doc: A short alias sets the flag it belongs to, recorded under the flag's name.
`-j8` binds the rest of the token. mise relies on this for `-C/tmp` and `-Edev`.
An attached value keeps every character after the flag letter, including leading slashes and equals-free punctuation.
`-j=8` binds `8`, not `=8`. A single leading `=` is a separator, matching the long form.
A value-taking short at the end of the command line is an error.
Value-less shorts may share a token: `-ab` sets both.
A bundle may end with a value-taking short, which then consumes the remainder of the token.
A token containing an unrecognized letter is not a bundle at all, so none of its letters are applied — `-az` does not set `-a`. Here it becomes a word, and there is no argument to hold it.

The same rejection, seen from the side that matters: with an argument free to take the token, `-a` must still be unset. A token containing an unrecognized letter was never a bundle, so none of its letters apply — the previous vector cannot show this, because both readings produce the same error.
A `count` flag records how many times it appeared, so `-vvv` is three.
The same count reached through separate tokens gives the same result.
A lone `-` is a value, conventionally meaning stdin, not a flag.
An unrecognized short flag is a word too, for the same reason as the long form.
Refusing unknown flags, an unrecognized letter fails the whole token rather than applying the letters before it — a partly-applied bundle would be worse than a rejected one.
`-1x` is not a number, so it is a flag-shaped token that names nothing — a CLI refusing unknown flags hears about it rather than having it slip through as a value.
